title: Honeycrisp Apple Growth Rates Increase "bitter pit" Disorder
content: New research indicates that accelerated growth rates in Honeycrisp apples exacerbate the "bitter pit" disorder, increasing both its incidence and severity. This costly dead-tissue condition contributes to significant fruit yield losses and avoidable economic impacts for apple producers and storers.
summary: New research shows that faster growth rates in Honeycrisp apples increase both the incidence and severity of the "bitter pit" disorder. The disorder causes large-scale fruit yield losses and avoidable economic impacts for apple producers and storers.
author: Phys.org

title: Technion team uses shaped laser pulses to steer ultrafast electron flow in STM
content: Researchers have combined the ability to image individual atoms with the capacity to capture electron motion at ultrafast timescales. A Technion‑led team achieved this in a scanning tunneling microscope by employing carefully shaped laser pulses to steer electron flow while maintaining nanoscale spatial resolution.
summary: Researchers combined atomic‑scale imaging with ultrafast timing in a scanning tunneling microscope. The Technion‑led team used carefully shaped laser pulses to control the direction of electron flow while preserving nanoscale spatial resolution.
author: Phys.org

title: Study: Climate change linked to two-thirds of 50,000 heat deaths in Europe
content: A new study reports that record-breaking heat in Europe this summer contributed to the deaths of more than 50,000 people. The research attributes nearly two-thirds of this mortality to human-caused climate change.
summary: A new study found that record heat in Europe this summer helped kill more than 50,000 people. Nearly two-thirds of that death toll was attributed to human-caused climate change.
author: Phys.org

title: Only 3.2% of glaciers, ending in lakes or oceans, lost over half of global ice loss
content: A new study reveals that glaciers terminating in lakes, oceans, or ice shelves represent just 3.2% of the world’s glaciers. Despite their small proportion, these glaciers lost 134 billion metric tons of ice annually between 2000 and 2019. This loss accounts for more than half of total global glacier ice loss during that period.
summary: Glaciers ending in lakes, oceans or ice shelves comprise 3.2% of the world's glaciers. They lost 134 billion metric tons (148 billion tons) of ice each year between 2000 and 2019, accounting for more than half of all glacier ice loss, according to a new study.
author: Phys.org

title: Red crown rot surges across Illinois as plant pathologist leads research
content:
Red crown rot, a fungal disease affecting soybean crops, is experiencing a surge across the Midwest after its initial report in Illinois in 2018. Boris Camiletti, a plant pathologist at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, is leading efforts to understand and combat the disease.

This initiative involves collaboration with the Crop Protection Network, the Illinois Soybean Association, the United Soybean Board, and researchers from surrounding states.
summary: Red crown rot, a fungal disease of soybean, is not new to the Midwest. First reported in Illinois in 2018, the disease is now surging across the state and the region.
author: Phys.org

title: AI agents form political camps and resist view changes in Nature Communications study
content: A recent experiment published in Nature Communications demonstrated that AI agents assigned political positions and tasked with defending their views formed distinct political camps. Over repeated exchanges, the agents increasingly preferred interacting with those holding similar opinions. The study found that simply changing the agents' conversation partners did little to soften these hardened views.
summary: A recent experiment published in Nature Communications found that AI agents assigned political positions formed opposing camps over repeated exchanges. The study showed that changing the agents' conversation partners did little to soften their established views.
author: Phys.org

title: Study Finds Men Dominant in Spanish AI Media Coverage, Women Only 5%
content: A new report titled "InfoIA: Analysis of Information on Artificial Intelligence Published in Digital Media" reveals a significant gender disparity in Spanish news coverage of artificial intelligence. Conducted by the University Institute of Gender Studies at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M), the study identifies a media "glass ceiling" in recent AI-related stories. The findings indicate that men are the primary subjects in 41% of these news reports, whereas women feature as main subjects in only 5% of the cases.
summary: Study Finds Men Dominant in Spanish AI Media Coverage, Women Only 5%.
author: Phys.org

title: Why do mathematicians keep proving things they already know?
content: Columnist Jacob Aron examines the nature of mathematical proofs, detailing how mathematicians approach open questions. He highlights that discovering multiple solutions to a single problem is a significant component of the broader mathematical endeavor.
summary: Why do mathematicians keep proving things they already know?
author: New Scientist

title: Computational method reveals underestimated energy-loss mechanism in silicon carbide defects
content:
Researchers have addressed a longstanding challenge in understanding how tiny defects in materials such as diamond and silicon carbide behave under light exposure. By developing a new computational method, the team identified a significant energy-loss mechanism in silicon carbide that had previously been underestimated by scientists. This discovery resolves a mystery that has persisted for years within the field.

The findings provide new insights into the behavior of these defects and may enhance the design of quantum computers and sensors. The work highlights the importance of accurate computational models in predicting material properties for advanced quantum technologies.
summary: Researchers solved a long-standing challenge in understanding how tiny defects in materials like diamond and silicon carbide behave when exposed to light. Their new computational method revealed a surprisingly important energy-loss mechanism in silicon carbide that scientists had previously underestimated, which could improve the design of quantum computers and sensors.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find sophisticated messaging system in hidden brain region
content:
Scientists have uncovered a hidden messaging system in a tiny region deep within the brain.  
Unlike the previously assumed uniform chemical broadcast, this area sends targeted signals that help regulate learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research conducted in mice.
summary: A tiny region deep within the brain reveals a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Unlike previously thought, the region sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.
author: Science Daily

title: Seven-Year Study Finds Exercise Slows Cognitive Decline in Parkinson’s Patients
content: A seven-year study reveals that increased physical activity among people with Parkinson’s disease is associated with slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Participants who exercised more than eight hours per week experienced almost no average cognitive decline, indicating that staying active may provide significant benefits as the disease progresses.
summary: A seven-year study found that people with Parkinson’s disease who were more physically active experienced slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Those exercising more than eight hours per week showed almost no average cognitive decline, suggesting that staying active may offer important benefits as the disease progresses.
author: Science Daily

title: MIT engineers build light-controlled swimming robot using living muscle cells
content: MIT engineers have developed a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that react to light flashes. This design enables the device to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough may facilitate the creation of tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that standard machines cannot safely navigate.
summary: MIT engineers have created a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light. This technology could enable the development of self-healing biological robots for exploring fragile environments.
author: Science Daily

title: FDA-Cleared PTSD Treatment Shows 68% Remission in Trial
content:
A newly FDA‑cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity in a clinical trial.

The trial reported a 52 % reduction in symptoms and a 68 % remission rate. Researchers say the technology could transform PTSD care and enable more precise treatments for other mental‑health conditions.
summary: The FDA-cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity. A clinical trial reported a 52% reduction in symptoms and 68% remission, and researchers believe the technology could transform PTSD care and pave the way for more precise treatments for other mental health conditions.
author: Science Daily

title: Dental Implants Release Particles That Hijack Immune System, Study Finds
content: Researchers have found that dental implant infections can resist antibiotics because the implants themselves contribute to the problem. Bacteria corrode titanium implants, releasing microscopic particles that hijack immune cells, trigger destructive inflammation, and accelerate jawbone loss.
summary: Researchers discovered that bacteria corroding titanium dental implants release microscopic particles that hijack immune cells. These particles trigger destructive inflammation and accelerate jawbone loss, contributing to antibiotic-resistant infections.
author: Science Daily

title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in five years
content: Switzerland’s glaciers are shrinking rapidly, with the country losing more than 5 % of its ice volume in 2026 alone. Several of the nation’s most famous glaciers recorded their worst melting on record, and several smaller glaciers have disappeared completely. Nearly 20 % of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.
summary: Switzerland’s glaciers have lost more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.
author: Science Daily

title: Kikai Caldera's Magma Reservoir Refilled 7,300 Years After Major Eruption
content:
Scientists have discovered that a massive magma reservoir beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera is refilling, 7,300 years after one of the planet’s most powerful volcanic eruptions. Using underwater seismic surveys, researchers identified a vast store of magma that appears to have accumulated since the ancient catastrophe.  

The finding may shed light on how supervolcanoes such as Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies, offering new insight into the long‑term dynamics of these powerful volcanic systems.
summary: Scientists used underwater seismic surveys to discover a massive magma reservoir beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera that is refilling 7,300 years after a major eruption. The finding may help explain how supervolcanoes such as Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies.
author: Science Daily

title: Mass General Brigham AI model predicts cancer survival from selfies
content: Take a selfie to see how healthy you are: the idea is enticing and this new research is promising. But so many factors have been ignored The idea that a single selfie could predict how long someone with cancer may live sounds like an incredible breakthrough. AI is getting better at spotting patterns in medical data, but can it be used to reliably predict what will happen to an individual patient? I asked a clinical colleague what she thought about the recent headlines. She found it an interesting development given that doctors have long used facial appearance to assess patient health. For example, she noted that they may write “appears stated age” or “appears older than stated age” as a proxy for general health. Now, researchers from Mass General Brigham, a healthcare institution in Massachusetts, have taken this idea a step further. They have developed an AI model trained on more than 40 million facial images – called FAHR-Face – to assess biological age and predict survival in cancer patients. For biological age, they developed FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates age from certain facial features such as the forehead, the wrinkles between the nose and mouth and the temples. For cancer survival, they developed FAHR-FaceSurvival, trained using almost 35,000 photos of cancer patients. This model focused more closely on the area below the eyes and the bridge of the nose – regions of the face “ linked with dying ”. Dr Raymond Mak, one of the study’s authors, noted that these parts of the face are the same as those referenced by Hippocrates in 400BC as signs of muscle wasting and mortality risk: “the nose sharp, the eyes sunken, the temples fallen in”. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
summary: Researchers at Mass General Brigham trained an AI model called FAHR‑Face on more than 40 million facial images to estimate biological age and predict cancer survival. The FAHR‑FaceSurvival submodel uses nearly 35,000 photos of cancer patients, focusing on facial regions linked to mortality risk.
author: Guardian Science

title: CoastSnap: Citizen Scientists Use Phone Cameras to Track Global Shoreline Changes
content:
Citizen scientists are now helping researchers monitor coastal changes using only an app and a camera phone. The program places a phone cradle and a sign at more than 200 spots worldwide, where participants can take a picture of the shoreline and send it to the project’s database.

Because shoreline positions shift with weather, tracking those changes over time is labor‑intensive. By encouraging everyday beachgoers to capture photos, the project turns a large workforce of camera‑phone users into a valuable resource for scientists.

The CoastSnap initiative began in Australia in 2017 and has since expanded to beaches around the globe. Each station includes a cradle to hold the phone while the photo is taken and a sign that explains where to send the snapshot.
summary: The CoastSnap project uses an app and a camera phone to capture shoreline photos at more than 200 spots worldwide, helping researchers monitor coastal changes. Started in Australia in 2017, the project now includes a cradle for phones and a sign that directs participants to send their snaps.
author: Guardian Science

title: Personalised mRNA vaccine intismeran cuts melanoma recurrence and death risk in trial
content:
A new clinical trial shows that a personalized mRNA‑based melanoma vaccine, intismeran, significantly reduces the risk of cancer recurrence or death within two years. The vaccine is custom‑made to target genetic mutations unique to each patient’s melanoma. Researchers described the results as a “foundational shift” in cancer treatment, highlighting the ability to harness the immune system in a more individualized manner.

Intismeran is the first individualized cancer vaccine to achieve positive outcomes in a phase III trial, marking the first time such a vaccine has demonstrated efficacy at this stage of testing.
summary: A personalised mRNA melanoma vaccine called intismeran, designed to target each patient’s unique tumor mutations, significantly reduced the risk of cancer recurrence or death within two years in a clinical trial. It is the first individualised cancer vaccine to show positive results in a phase III trial.
author: Guardian Science

title: Creator builds custom TV software with ML models after unwanted webOS update
content: A recent (unwanted) webOS update that got installed on TV prompted me to start going down the rabbit hole of writing new TV software. After a couple of weekends and massive help from 4 different models, finally managed to get v1 working. My daughter enjoys navigating TV through speech while I get to browse on the biggest screen at home. While all of the code was written by ML models, there were decisions I had to help with. In specific: using WebRTC to cut down latency, repurposing vendor logic for buffering voice samples and designing user experience. It was liberating to finally free the TV of bloatware and make it truly personalized! Comments URL: https://news. Ycombinator. Com/item? Id=50202865 Points: 28 # Comments: 3
summary: The author wrote new TV software (v1) after an unwanted webOS update, with code generated by machine‑learning models and testing on four different TV models. The implementation uses WebRTC to reduce latency, repurposes vendor logic for buffering voice samples, and enables speech navigation and browsing on the TV screen.
author: Hacker News

title: Apple launches its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo
content: Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, has been released, prompting readers to consider whether they obtained it on launch day or are still deliberating. The accompanying piece promises to outline eight key points to keep in mind about the new device.
summary: Apple released its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo. The article provides several points to consider about the device.
author: Wired

title: TDM Neo Hybrid Headphones Review Highlights Engineering Praise and Sound Disappointment
content: At CES 2026, the TDM Neo Hybrid headphones were highlighted for their ability to convert into a Bluetooth speaker. After extended use, the reviewer says the engineering impresses them, but the sound quality falls short of expectations.
summary: CES 2026 highlighted the TDM Neo Hybrid headphones, which transform into a Bluetooth speaker. The reviewer was impressed by the engineering but less impressed by the sound.
author: Wired

title: iPhone Duo is not a small phone, unlike iPhone 13 Mini
content:
The recent review of the iPhone Duo clarifies that the device is not a small phone, despite its 5.4‑inch cover screen. The author notes that among the devices shown, only the iPhone 13 Mini on the left qualifies as truly small.

Readers who follow the iPhone 13 Mini expressed hope that the Duo might serve as a compact phone that expands into a tablet, but the review states that the Duo is “thick and heavy.” The author describes feeling its weight during everyday tasks such as reading email, scrolling Instagram, or placing it in a pocket, and characterizes it as a dense phone.

The reviewer also mentions personal use of an iPhone 13 Mini, which they keep despite its limited battery life that “barely lasts a full day.” The overall conclusion is that the iPhone Duo does not meet the expectations of Mini fans seeking a small, lightweight handset.
summary: The iPhone Duo is not a small phone despite its Mini‑ish 5.4‑inch cover screen. It is thick, heavy and feels dense when used, unlike the truly small iPhone 13 Mini.
author: The Verge

title: Warhound startup to genetically modify dogs and add Anduril tech
content:
Warhound, a Texas‑based defense startup, has announced plans to genetically enhance military and police dogs and equip them with Anduril’s military technology. The company, founded by Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Ben Lamm—co‑founder of Colossal Biosciences—has already secured $200 million in funding.  

Warhound will use Colossal Biosciences’ expertise in genetics, cloning, and animal biology to produce healthier dogs with traits suited to demanding missions. Anduril will then outfit the animals with its “advanced cybernetic Augments.” The Warhound website describes the initiative as “a new breed of dominance.”
summary: Warhound, a Texas‑based defense startup founded by Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences co‑founder Ben Lamm, has raised $200 million. The company plans to genetically modify military and police dogs and outfit them with Anduril’s advanced cybernetic Augments.
author: The Verge

title: Influential voices warn AI may trigger massive crises, citing Friedman's crisis theory
content:
An old policy concept is reappearing in public debate as a group of influential voices warns that artificial‑intelligence development may trigger crises of vast magnitude. The discussion centers on whether a guaranteed‑employment program could address potential mass AI‑related unemployment.

The conversation cites a passage from Milton Friedman’s preface to Capitalism and Freedom, in which he observed that “only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change” and that crises can bring once‑fringe ideas into the political mainstream. Friedman added that the role of intellectuals, think‑tanks and economists is to refine such ideas so that “good ones are ready when disaster strikes.”
summary: Influential voices predict that artificial intelligence could cause crises of vast magnitude. American economist Milton Friedman observed that crises bring fringe ideas into the mainstream and that intellectuals should refine ideas for disaster response.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 offers longer battery life but still lacks new features
content: Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI As the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative. That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model. summary: The Apple Watch Ultra 4, Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch, receives a battery and chip boost that extends battery life while otherwise remaining similar to last year’s model. Several key features announced for Apple’s 2026 smartwatch lineup are still disabled and are expected to be enabled in updates later this year.

title: Albania's parliament erupts in chaos as MPs clash amid tenth‑day student protests
content:
Heated exchanges and chaotic scenes gripped Albania’s parliament in Tirana on Thursday as rival MPs clashed inside.  

Student demonstrators continued their protests outside the building for a tenth consecutive day.
summary: Heated exchanges and chaotic scenes occurred inside Albania's parliament in Tirana on Thursday as rival MPs clashed. Student demonstrators continued their protests outside the building for a tenth day.
author: Euronews

title: Flash floods swamp southeast Australia, force school closures; reporter rescues driver
content: Flash floods have swamped southeast Australia, with record October rainfall prompting widespread school closures. In Morayfield, Queensland, a television reporter abandoned his shoes and glasses, diving into rising floodwaters to rescue a driver whose car was rapidly sinking.
summary: Flash floods across southeast Australia, driven by record October rainfall, have forced school closures. A television reporter in Morayfield, Queensland, abandoned his shoes and glasses and entered rising floodwaters to rescue a driver whose car was sinking.
author: Euronews

title: Oil spill reaches Umm Al Quwain beaches after tanker hit by projectile off UAE coast
content: Oil spill has reached UAE beaches, prompting the Ministry of Climate Change to deploy teams to contain the spill on Umm Al Quwain. The incident follows a tanker struck by a projectile off the UAE coast, which ignited a fire, amid a rise in tanker attacks near Hormuz.
summary: The UAE’s Ministry of Climate Change said teams were deployed to contain a spill affecting Umm Al Quwain’s beaches. The spill came days after a tanker was struck by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire.
author: Euronews

title: Trump says he can run for a third term in 2028, claims 2020 election was stolen
content: U.S. President Donald Trump reiterated that he believes he can pursue a third presidential term in 2028, contending that the 2020 election was stolen. He made the claim despite the Constitution’s two‑term limit for presidents.
summary: US President Donald Trump said he could run for a third term in 2028. He argued the 2020 election was stolen despite the US Constitution's two-term limit.

content: A midday news bulletin for October 23, 2026 invites audiences to catch up with the most important stories from Europe and beyond. The bulletin promises coverage of the latest and breaking news across world, business, entertainment, politics, culture and travel topics.

author: Euronews

title: Explosion at private coal mine in northern Turkey kills two, traps one
content: An explosion at a privately owned coal mine in northern Turkey killed two miners and injured five others, two of them seriously. Authorities report that one person remains trapped inside the mine.
summary: Two miners were killed and five injured, two of them seriously, in an explosion at a privately owned mine in northern Turkey. One person is still trapped inside the mine.

title: UN seeks new Secretary-General as Antonio Guterres' term ends
content: Antonio Guterres’s term as United Nations Secretary‑General is ending, prompting the organization to begin the search for his successor. According to France 24’s New York correspondent Jessica Le Masurier, leading candidates are encountering difficulty in securing the necessary support.
summary: Antonio Guterres's term as UN Secretary-General is coming to an end. Leading candidates are struggling to secure the support needed as the UN looks for his replacement.

title: Claude Monet's 'Iris' sells for 50 million euros, France's record auction price
content: Claude Monet’s monumental Impressionist painting “Iris” sold for 50 million euros, including buyer’s fees, at a Paris auction on Thursday. The sale set a new record as the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction in France.
summary: Claude Monet's monumental painting "Iris" sold for 50 million euros, including buyer fees, at a Paris auction on Thursday. The sale set a record as the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction in France.
author: France 24

title: French authorities ask public to submit looting videos to identify rioters
content: French authorities are asking anyone who recorded footage of looting during last weekend’s riots across France to submit their videos to aid the investigation. Officials describe the request as unprecedented, and the move has sparked debate.
summary: French authorities are requesting people who filmed looting scenes across France last weekend to hand in their videos to aid identification of rioters. The request is described as an unprecedented decision and has sparked debate.
author: France 24

content: Claude Monet’s monumental painting “Iris” sold for 50 million euros (about $56 million) at an auction in Paris on Thursday, setting a new record as the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction in France.

content: French prosecutors said they are treating a shooting in Trappes, west of Paris, as a suspected terrorist attack. The incident occurred earlier in the day when a man fired from a vehicle, killing at least one person and wounding four others.
summary: French prosecutors said they are investigating a shooting in Trappes, west of Paris, as a suspected terrorist attack. The attack killed at least one person and wounded four after a man opened fire from a vehicle.
author: France 24

title: South Africa investigates foreign national's murder during Durban anti-immigrant protests
content: South African police are investigating the murder of a foreign national after violent anti‑immigrant protests swept through Durban’s central business district. The killing follows months of rallies in which at least ten foreigners have been killed, prompting several other African nations to repatriate their citizens. The incident was reported by France 24’s correspondent Eunice Masson.
summary: South African police are investigating the murder of a foreign national after violent anti‑immigrant protests swept the central business district of Durban. The killing follows months of rallies that have left at least ten foreigners dead and prompted several African countries to repatriate their citizens.
author: France 24

title: French authorities ban some student protests after weekend looting and clashes
content: French authorities imposed bans on some student protests after a weekend of clashes and widespread looting that was described as the most violent unrest in years. Nonetheless, dozens of protesters took to the streets of Paris on Thursday, defying the demonstration bans ordered in multiple French cities.
summary: The bans on demonstrations were ordered in multiple French cities after a weekend of clashes and widespread looting that marked France’s most violent unrest in years. Dozens of protesters still took to the streets in Paris on Thursday despite the bans.
author: France 24

title: Sri Lanka’s largest elephant dies, highlighting human‑elephant conflict
content: The death of an elephant believed to be Sri Lanka’s largest has highlighted concerns over human‑elephant conflict in the country’s rural areas. Sri Lanka experiences a high number of deadly encounters between people and elephants, underscoring ongoing habitat challenges.
summary: The death of what was thought to be Sri Lanka’s largest elephant has drawn attention to human‑elephant conflict in rural communities. Sri Lanka sees a high number of deadly encounters between people and elephants.

title: Andy Burnham warns of a winter of greater flooding amid emergency preparedness talks
content: The prime minister said the government is having conversation about emergency preparedness A DUP minister has said he is confident MP Carla Lockhart will stay in the party despite leaving its main decision-making body amid a row with party leadership over the future of Stormont. author: Guardian World

title: India to cut prices of 137 cancer drugs after Supreme Court calls mark‑ups extortion
content: Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court. From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.
summary: The Indian government will lower the price of 137 cancer drugs starting next month after a Supreme Court ruling that described mark‑ups as “extortion”. The decision follows a 2022 case filed by a retired bank clerk who could not afford her medicine and is intended to help poorer patients facing high treatment costs.
author: Guardian World

title: Finnish 24‑hour TV livestream of newborn puppies draws millions of viewers
content:
A Finnish television program that streams a dog and her six newborn puppies around the clock is attracting millions of viewers. The 24‑hour show, called Pentulive (Puppy Live), offers a continuous webcam feed of the litter’s development.

In addition to the live video, the broadcast provides evening chat sessions with the breeder, a dedicated podcast and an instant‑notification service that informs followers of milestones such as birth, weigh‑ins and the puppies’ first nail trims for an eight‑week period.
summary: A 24‑hour Finnish TV show follows a dog and her six newborn puppies, attracting millions of viewers. The show offers a webcam, evening chat with the breeder, a podcast and notifications on milestones such as weigh‑ins and nail trims for eight weeks.
author: Guardian World

title: AfD internal leak shows party’s decade‑long effort to court Trump and MAGA allies
content: Documents show German party’s scramble to request support after president’s 2016 election win and co-leader’s pursuit of Steve Bannon A data leak from Germany’s far-right German Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has revealed the extent of efforts by the party to court Donald Trump and other leading figures in the Maga movement, stretching back more than a decade. The trove also reveals the pains the AfD took in wooing the president, whom they saw from the beginning as a potential ally, with senior party officials agonising over the wording of an obsequious congratulatory telegram when he was elected in 2016, which included the wish that his “hopes as a person be fulfilled”.
summary: AfD internal leak shows party’s decade‑long effort to court Trump and MAGA allies.
author: Guardian World

title: French interior minister vows uncompromising stance on vandals before weekend protests
content:
French interior minister Laurent Nuñez said authorities will be “uncompromising” with “vandals” ahead of upcoming weekend protests and defended blanket bans on demonstrations in some parts of France.  

In a separate statement, French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu addressed a shooting that occurred this morning in the towns of Trappes and La Verrière, west of Paris. The attack left one person dead and four injured. Police reported that the gunman was arrested in nearby Coignières.
summary: Laurent Nuñez defended blanket bans on demonstrations in some parts of France. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu issued a statement after a shooting in Trappes and La Verrière that left one person dead and four injured, and the gunman was arrested in Coignières.
author: Guardian World

title: Duchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against father
content:
The Duchess of Sussex, Meghan, said she is “deeply distressed” after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half‑brother, Thomas Markle Jr., alleged he had found a stash of child sexual abuse images belonging to their estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr. at his former home in the Philippines.

title: Dudeney wins epic as British trio reach Wrexham Open quarter-finals
content: Alicia Dudeney secured a victory on day three of the Wrexham Open, joining British players Jodie Burrage and Hannah Klugman in the quarter-finals. The result marked a strong performance for the trio during the tournament's progression.
summary: Alicia Dudeney defeated her opponent on day three of the Wrexham Open to advance to the quarter-finals. She joins Jodie Burrage and Hannah Klugman in the next round, marking a strong performance for British players.

title: Heat killed record 50,000 people in European cities this summer, scientists warn
content:
Heat killed a record 50,000 people in European cities this summer, new research shows, with scientists attributing two in every three of the deaths to climate breakdown. The study notes that the highest fatality rates occurred in Malta, Italy and Hungary, where health issues, loneliness and poverty amplified the toll.

From June to August, morgues and funeral homes were overwhelmed as the heat, intensified by planet‑baking pollution, cut short an additional 32,000 lives in urban areas. Researchers found that hot days pushed vulnerable bodies into overdrive while warm nights prevented recovery, contributing to the surge in deaths.

title: Cardiac MRI identifies distinct filling mechanisms in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

The imaging techniques reveal alterations associated with different mechanisms of impaired cardiac filling, while the heart’s pumping function remains largely maintained.

The study, titled DECIPHER HFpEF, was published in JACC: Cardiovascular Imaging. It highlights that MRI can detect tissue changes that explain why patients with HFpEF experience inadequate filling despite preserved ejection fraction.

title: MIT professor traces AI’s roots to early engineers injecting randomness
content:
Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in MIT’s History Section and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, has explored the roots of modern artificial intelligence in a new paper published in Past and Present. In the article, Lindquist argues that early AI pioneers deliberately introduced randomness into deterministic algorithms to emulate the “messy” aspects of human thought. He traces the origins of what contemporary developers call AI hallucinations to these early experiments and warns that a balance between creativity and predictability will always be difficult to achieve.

Lindquist explains that the idea of injecting irrationality into machines was influenced by a broader mid‑century belief that chance plays a key role in discovery and artistic creation. He cites John Pierce, a prominent Bell Labs electrical engineer, who argued that mathematics could remove order from art and add unexpected bursts of irregularity. Early neural networks, built by psychologists, were intended to model the brain and reveal how it makes productive mistakes. These systems were not viewed as black boxes; researchers hoped they would provide insight into the messy processes of the mind. A competing view held that creative thinking was simply “normal” thinking performed more efficiently, and the debate centered on how to replicate human inventiveness in machine form.

According to Lindquist, the way early engineers approached AI differs from today’s focus on correctness. Early neural networks were prized for producing surprising, sometimes bizarre answers, whereas modern systems like ChatGPT or Claude are valued for giving reliable, expected responses. The shift has been driven in part by legal and monetary concerns that discourage unexpected or erroneous outputs.

Lindquist traces the historical trajectory of neural networks, noting that symbolic AI—an approach that represents knowledge in rules and propositions—dominated until the 1980s. The death of Frank Rosenblatt, a key figure in neural network research, in 1971 coincided with the rise of symbolic AI, though neural networks persisted in cognitive science. The availability of large data sets and increased computing power with the internet, and a breakthrough in 2012 when neural networks began outperforming statistical machine learning, shifted the field back toward data‑driven models.

Finally, Lindquist cautions that attempts to eliminate hallucinations may come at the cost of creativity. He stresses that the historical experience shows a trade‑off: making AI more predictable can unintentionally reduce its capacity for surprising, creative insights.
summary: Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in MIT History Section, says early AI pioneers injected randomness into algorithms to mimic human creativity and produce hallucinations. He argues that tradeoffs between creativity and predictability will persist as AI systems are refined.

title: 2026 El Niño Mirrors 1997 Event, NASA Altimetry Shows Rising Sea Levels
content:
El Niño Then and Now

NASA Earth Observatory has released a pair of sea‑surface‑height maps that compare the 2026 El Niño event with the 1997‑98 and 2015‑16 outbreaks. The 2026 map, taken on October 12, shows higher‑than‑normal sea levels across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, a classic hallmark of El Niño. The pattern is almost identical to the October 13, 1997 map, which was captured during one of the strongest El Niño events recorded by satellite altimetry.

The altimetry data come from TOPEX/Poseidon for 1997, Jason‑2 for 2015, and the Sentinel‑6 Michael Freilich satellite for 2026. All three datasets were processed by scientists at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). The maps illustrate sea‑level anomalies in shades of red (higher than average), white (normal), and blue (lower). Seasonal cycles and long‑term trends were removed so that the anomalies associated with El Niño and other short‑term natural phenomena stand out.

Josh Willis, JPL’s project scientist for sea‑level missions, notes that the 2026 event arrived more suddenly than the 1997‑98 event, but the two now appear similar in character. Both show a tilt of sea level—low in the west and high in the east—and high, warm water extending to South America. Willis suggests that the impacts could be comparable, citing the heavy rains that fell in California and the southern United States during the 1997‑98 event.

The 2015‑16 El Niño, while also strong, had a different pattern. The warm, high water along the equator did not reach the coast of South America to the same extent, producing rainfall that concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern United States. This difference is visible in the altimetry map for October 12, 2015, which shows a less pronounced elevation along the South American coast.

NOAA’s El Niño outlook released on October 8, 2026, called for an 83 percent chance of a strong‑to‑very strong El Niño through the first three months of 2027. Willis cautions that the chaotic nature of the atmosphere can alter the eventual impacts, noting that “just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.”
summary: 2026 El Niño Mirrors 1997 Event, NASA Altimetry Shows Rising Sea Levels.

title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review highlights North Korean invasion storyline
content: Activision; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game And so we return perhaps one final time to Call of Duty’s Modern Warfare strand, with stories, “ripped from the newspaper headlines”, featuring shady terror organisations, nefarious rogue states and the brutally capable, monosyllabic war fighters who stand between us and Armageddon. Last year’s Black Ops 7 instalment was a sales disappointment for Activision, and that has no doubt put extra pressure on Infinity Ward, the studio leading Modern Warfare 4 development. Fortunately, this developer – like series heroes Price, Gaz and Ghost – seems to thrive on pressure. As you may have read, this year’s campaign is based around a fictitious North Korean ruling family that has seized an opportunity to invade its southern neighbour. Amid the chaos, a small group of Korean and American marines must help lead the fightback, while in the shadows, SAS hard man John Price makes an unlikely new comrade in his own morally ambiguous quest to put the world to rights. Mads Mikkelsen pops up as evil mastermind The Archer, but like Kiernan Shipka in Black Ops 7 he’s rather wasted, with very little screen time.
summary: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review highlights North Korean invasion storyline.

content:

title: Leander Schaerlaeckens: Trump’s Fifa peace prize was a sham
content: The first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccer Sign up for our free newsletter here Poor Fifa peace prize. Unloved, unliked, mocked, tainted by association with its first winner. And now demoted, too, after Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, dumped the thing on the global governing body’s “social responsibility committee” to look after. To redeem it, rather than to ditch it, to spare Infantino the embarrassment of acknowledging that his fake prize was really just a fake prize all along. Here is where we should probably acknowledge that, as fake prizes go, and in the context of what it was intended to accomplish, the first awarding of the Fifa peace prize was an unqualified success. It achieved exactly what it was meant to, made by Infantino to flatter Donald Trump, the man he needed to keep on his side to safeguard the riches to be extracted from the North American market in order to consolidate his power base within Fifa. Trump, the gullible buffoon, was pleased as punch – handed a big, golden bauble and a medal he placed around his own neck – and briefly forgot about the Nobel peace prize he desperately covets. Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.
summary: Author Leander Schaerlaeckens argues that the first Fifa peace prize awarded to Donald Trump was a fabricated creation by Gianni Infantino designed to flatter the former president. The article suggests that while the initial award was a sham, a reimagined version of the prize could still hold meaning for the soccer world.

title: Nottingham Forest's poor start focuses attention on Glasner and Delap
content:

The team’s struggles are highlighted by defensive and offensive difficulties at home, where they have scored zero goals and secured only a single point at the City Ground.

The fates of Glasner and Delap are now closely linked as Forest prepares to face Ipswich, the club where Delap began his career. Despite the challenging position, the club is reportedly maintaining a calm demeanor. This approach reflects a deliberate effort to avoid the short-termism that plagued the previous season, during which Forest appointed a third head coach after a disappointing run.

The current situation follows a significant managerial change this summer, when the club replaced Vítor Pereira with Glasner. Although Pereira had successfully guided the team to safety from relegation, Forest’s owners viewed the opportunity to hire Glasner as a chance to elevate the squad’s performance, mirroring the transformation he previously achieved at Crystal Palace.
summary: Nottingham Forest sit 19th in the Premier League with zero home goals and one point, creating early pressure on manager Oliver Glasner and striker Liam Delap. title: Light-activated catalyst makes hydrogen peroxide production three times more efficient
content:

The development addresses the environmental footprint of current industrial processes, which are predominantly energy-intensive. The findings detailing this more efficient photocatalyst have been published in the journal Advanced Materials.

title: NASA estimates 22 Starship launches needed for lunar lander
content:
NASA has historically declined to disclose the precise number of Starship launches required to fuel a lunar lander for the Artemis Program, a metric the agency has guarded closely. The number of launches needed to propel a Starship-based lander from low-Earth orbit to the Moon, execute a landing, and return to lunar orbit has been a moving target for years. When pressed for specifics, NASA officials have typically responded that they do not know the exact figure and therefore will not provide one.

In 2023, Lisa Watson-Morgan, the then-director of NASA's Human Landing System, told Ars that while the agency had a general idea of the requirements, she was reluctant to state the exact number. The provided text indicates that the latest estimate for this requirement is 22 launches, though it notes that NASA does not possess or desire nuclear weapons, using that comparison to highlight the agency’s unusual secrecy regarding this specific logistical figure.
summary: NASA's latest estimate indicates that 22 Starship launches are required to fuel a Starship-based lunar lander in low-Earth orbit. This figure supports the Artemis Program's goal of landing people on the Moon and returning them to lunar orbit.

title: Switch 2 partially jailbroken via SmileBasic 4 integer overflow
content:
Security researcher Sammy Hajhamid has demonstrated a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Nintendo Switch 2, achieving "userland" access. According to Hajhamid, this vulnerability enables users to run homebrew software, reverse engineer and modify games, back up save files, and access most of the console’s peripherals through MMIO. The exploit relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, a programming environment and interpreter for Nintendo hardware.

The hack requires a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a specific node that facilitates privileged system access. Hajhamid developed a custom harness to send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI, using a Bluetooth light switch to power cycle the device. He utilized OpenAI's Codex to analyze SmileBasic’s language interpreter over a two-week period.

The process identified a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. This error provides access to an array pointer, which grants read and write access to portions of the system memory.
summary: Security researcher Sammy Hajhamid demonstrated a tethered software-only jailbreak for the Switch 2 using an integer overflow in SmileBasic 4. This exploit grants userland access to run homebrew, reverse engineer games, and back up save files.

title: After Starshield interruption, Ukraine wants to build its own satellite communication network with ICEYE and Nokia
content:
Ukraine has signed a letter of intent with Finnish telecommunications company Nokia and satellite manufacturer ICEYE to explore the development of a sovereign satellite-communications network. The agreement, announced on October 22, aims to establish secure, high-performance satellite systems that Ukraine fully controls. Rafal Modrzewski, ICEYE’s cofounder and CEO, stated that the company has a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions and has supported Ukraine since 2022. He emphasized the need for Ukraine to possess communications infrastructure it can rely on independently.

The move comes in response to recent disruptions in Ukraine’s access to existing satellite services. Ukraine currently relies heavily on SpaceX’s Starlink megaconstellation and Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink used by the U.S. Government and its allies. Starshield is particularly crucial for Ukraine, as it enables the operation of fast-moving drones over large distances in both offensive and defensive capacities. On October 14, Ukrainian soldiers and officials reported a severe throttling of Starshield services, which imposed speed limits on terminal-carrying drones and caused many to crash.

Responsibility for the throttling remains unclear. Some U.S. officials indicated the order came from Elon Musk, but Musk stated that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. In a post on X on October 14, Musk asserted that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately the President. The throttling appears to still be in effect, reinforcing Ukraine’s desire to control its own satellite-communications infrastructure.

Mikko Hautala, Nokia’s chief geopolitical and government relations officer and chairman of Nokia Defense, noted that satellite networks are key to secure communications when ground networks are disrupted. He stated that through the letter of intent, Nokia, Ukraine, and ICEYE will explore how trusted, sovereign satellite communications can strengthen Ukraine’s resilience. This partnership builds on an agreement announced on October 1 between Nokia and ICEYE to help nations develop similar sovereign systems.

ICEYE already supports the Ukrainian defense effort through its fleet of Earth-observing satellites in low Earth orbit, which use synthetic aperture radar. Ukraine utilizes data from the ICEYE constellation for intelligence and planning. This relationship has placed ICEYE in a vulnerable position, as a Russian inspector satellite named Kosmos 2612 recently made an extremely close approach to ICEYE-X36, a satellite operated by ICEYE US. The goal of this unsanctioned rendezvous is unclear, though it may have been intended to assess capabilities, interfere with the satellite, or send a message regarding Russia’s ability to interact with satellites.
summary: Ukraine wants its own satellite-communication system, which shouldn't be surprising given the events of the past week or so. The Ukrainian military just signed a letter of intent with two Finnish companies — the telecom giant Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE — to look into developing a sovereign satellite-communications network for Ukraine.

title: Space Shuttle Columbia carries Gene Roddenberry's ashes into space on STS-52
content: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of " Star Trek," aboard. During mission STS-52, NASA astronaut and shuttle commander James Wetherbee brought a small container with a portion of Roddenberry's ashes into space as part of his personal effects at the request of Roddenberry's widow, Majel Barrett. It was Roddenberry's lifelong dream to go to space, but he never got to go while he was alive. But thanks to his wife, a little bit of Roddenberry finally made it to space almost exactly one year after his death. NASA and his family didn't tell anyone about it until almost two years later in 1994. Wetherbee said he was "honored to be asked" by Barrett to carry Roddenberry's ashses on the spaceflight. "I'm just glad I was able to bring a little happiness to the family," he said, according to Newsweek. The Space Shuttle Columbia (STS-52) launches from NASA's Kennedy Space Center on Oct. 22, 1992. (Image credit: NASA) Here's why it mattered The launch of Roddenberry's ashes into space on NASA's STS-52 mission aboard the space shuttle Columbia marked the world's first " space burial," but it wouldn't be the last. About five years after Roddenberry's memorial flight, in 1997, the space memorial company Celestis began launching a series of "burial" flights by flying capsules with human cremains on rockets. In fact, more of Roddenberry's ashes flew on Celestis' "founders flight" in April 1997 aboard an air-launched Pegasus rocket that took off from the Canary Islands in Spain. The ashes of Roddenberry's wife and of Star Trek actor James Dooha n have also flown in space, among others. Celestis has gone on to launch human cremains on many suborbital and orbital flights, including some on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets. The company even launched the ashes of the late astronomer Eugene Shoemaker to the moon in 1999 on the Luna 1 flight, with another set of cremains launched into deep space on the Enterprise mission in 2023. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.
summary: On Oct. 22, 1992, NASA shuttle Columbia on mission STS-52 carried a small container of Gene Roddenberry’s ashes into space. The ashes were placed aboard at the request of his widow Majel Barrett and were later disclosed in 1994, marking the first space burial.

title: Europe's Space Rider vehicle comes crashing down during drop test
content:
On October 6, the European Space Agency (ESA) conducted a full-scale drop test of its Space Rider prototype at a military range on the Italian island of Sardinia. The minivan-sized mockup was released from a helicopter at an altitude of approximately 2 miles (3 kilometers) to evaluate the vehicle’s descent and landing systems. While the initial drogue parachute deployed successfully and began slowing the descent, the main steerable parafoil detached during its deployment sequence. This anomaly left the prototype unable to slow its descent further, resulting in a crash into the ground.

The failure occurred during a system-level test intended to demonstrate Space Rider’s ability to perform runway-style touchdowns using its wingless, lifting-body design. According to an ESA spokesperson, the test was not completed as planned due to the issue with the parafoil. An independent investigation is currently ongoing to determine the root cause of the failure and to inform the next steps in the development process. ESA officials confirmed that all components of the craft have been recovered following the incident.

Géraldine Naja, ESA’s director of space transportation, addressed the event during an ESA Council media briefing on October 22. She described the incident as an unfortunate but important part of space system development, noting that many successful tests had preceded this attempt. Naja stated that the remaining qualification activities for Space Rider are not on the critical path of the vehicle’s development. Consequently, she expressed hope that this specific test failure would not damage or require modifications to the remaining schedule and qualification activities.

Space Rider is being developed as Europe’s first reusable, uncrewed orbital spacecraft, designed to carry scientific experiments to orbit for up to two months before returning them to Earth. Its unique landing method relies on a steerable parachute to maneuver toward a landing area, distinguishing it from other current spacecraft recovery practices. The descent and landing qualification campaign began in 2025, with previous successes demonstrating the vehicle’s autonomous capabilities and parafoil deployment.

The October 6 test was the first drop test since an unsuccessful attempt in May, when a sensor flagged an issue during preparations, leading engineers to abort the test before release. Following that incident, the testing range operated by Italy’s Ministry of Defense was unavailable from June through September. Beyond landing systems, Space Rider underwent separate thermal protection testing earlier in the year, where heat-shield materials were exposed to temperatures around 2,900 degrees Fahrenheit (1,600 degrees Celsius) in plasma wind tunnel trials. ESA has targeted the vehicle’s first orbital mission for later this decade.
summary: Europe's Space Rider vehicle comes crashing down during drop test.

title: Billy Evans emerges as key villain in Elizabeth Holmes documentary
content:
Nathan Fielder’s documentary You Can See Everything has emerged as a surprise hit, featuring Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder currently serving a prison sentence for defrauding investors. The film also showcases Fielder, known for his comedy-reality series Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, as an on-camera co-director. While audiences are likely familiar with Holmes from her media coverage and the Hulu miniseries The Dropout, a third figure, Billy Evans, plays a significant role in the second half of the film.

Evans, Holmes’s partner, is described as a not-particularly-famous individual whose screen time competes with the three well-known faces in what is characterized as a four-character drama. Holmes has stated that she and Evans are not legally married, though they became engaged in 2018, have two children, and treat each other as spouses. Despite his lower profile, Evans is not excluded from the narrative in terms of screen time or memorability.

However, Evans remains the odd man out in the broader discourse surrounding the film. As You Can See Everything sparks conversations about manipulation, shifting sympathies, and trust, a consensus has formed among viewers regarding Evans. The source notes that in all the discussion prompted by the movie, everyone seems to agree on one crucial point: Billy Evans sucks. This reaction highlights how the film’s portrayal of Evans has become a focal point for audience engagement, distinguishing him from the other central figures in the documentary.
summary: Nathan Fielder’s documentary You Can See Everything identifies Elizabeth Holmes’s partner Billy Evans as a central figure in the film’s narrative. The article notes that viewers widely agree Evans is the film’s most untrustworthy character despite his lower public profile.

title: Study supports FDA approval of dolutegravir for HIV treatment in newborns
content:
An international study conducted through the International Maternal Pediatric Adolescent AIDS Clinical Trials (IMPAACT) Network, involving researchers at the University of California San Diego, helped inform the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s recent approval of dolutegravir. This second-generation integrase inhibitor is now approved for treating human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) in newborns from birth.

The study, published in The Lancet HIV, identified a specific dosing regimen that achieves appropriate drug levels in full-term newborns. These findings support the use of dolutegravir to treat HIV from the first days of life.
summary: An international study through the IMPAACT Network helped inform the FDA's recent approval of dolutegravir for treating HIV-1 in newborns. The research, published in The Lancet HIV, identified a dosing regimen that achieves appropriate drug levels in full-term newborns.

title: Meta revises terms but experts say AI can still scrape news sites
content:
Meta has modified its business terms to remove language that previously suggested it could freely train AI models on news sites, such as The Verge. However, legal experts argue these adjustments are insufficient to resolve their concerns. James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, told Nieman Lab that the changes do not restrict the "associated with your products or services" language, which would still permit Meta to scrape entire websites.

The new terms for business accounts, which take effect on October 30th, initially appeared to grant Meta permission to use news sites for AI training. Grimmelmann noted that the specific phrasing remains problematic, as it continues to allow for broad scraping activities despite the recent tweaks to the agreement.
summary: Meta has removed language from its business terms that suggested it could freely train AI models on news sites. content:

title: German photographer wins 2026 Nikon Small World for inkjet droplet image
content:
Ole Bielfeldt, a 25-year-old German experimental photographer, has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition. His winning image captures ink droplets being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer, a project that distinguished him from 1,802 other entries submitted from 69 countries. Bielfeldt discovered his interest in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown when he found an old microscope in his parents' attic. He subsequently taught himself the technique by building a custom adaptor from a tube and wood to connect the microscope to his father’s camera.

Capturing the rapid movement of ink droplets presented a significant technical challenge, as the drops moved faster than the camera’s standard shutter speed. To overcome this, Bielfeldt deconstructed the printer so that the paper moved beneath a stationary printhead. He then photographed the process in a dark room, using a flash to freeze the ink drops mid-air. Bielfeldt, who operates the photography and videography brand macrofying, relies on traditional techniques and does not use AI in his images.
summary: Ole Bielfeldt, a 25-year-old German experimental photographer, won the 2026 Nikon Small World competition with an image of ink droplets from an inkjet printer. He captured the fast-moving droplets by deconstructing the printer and using a flash to freeze the action in a dark room.

title: Vance Urges Republicans to Stop Whining Over Ramaswamy Attack Ad in Ohio Governor Race
content:
US Vice President JD Vance defended an attack ad released by Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign in the Ohio governor’s race on Wednesday. Vance told fellow Republicans to "stop whining" about the advertisement and focus on winning the election. The ad features Donna Arthur, the estranged mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton, who disputes Acton’s account of a childhood involving homelessness and sexual abuse. Arthur, whom Acton says she has not seen since 1978, urges Ohio voters not to support her daughter.

Acton has stated that she was sexually abused by her stepfather at age twelve. She noted that her mother remained with the stepfather, who was charged with rape but fled the state and was never tried before his death in 2004. Acton also claimed that she and her brother were removed from their mother's custody due to severe abuse, neglect, and sexual abuse, a narrative supported by her brother.

title: Israel’s Ben‑Gvir uses AI videos to mock Gazans as “donkeys” and send them to Paris
content:
Israel’s far‑right minister Itamar Ben‑Gvir has released a series of AI‑generated videos that mock Palestinians and push political messages ahead of the country’s election. The clips include scenes that magically transport Gazans to Paris and label them “donkeys” for choosing to stay in Gaza.

One of the videos has triggered an online spat with France. The incident highlights the growing use of AI in the campaign, as parties employ deepfakes, bots and other AI‑generated content, raising concerns about disinformation and the technology’s influence on voters.
summary: Israel’s far‑right minister Itamar Ben‑Gvir is using AI‑generated videos to mock Palestinians, including transporting Gazans to Paris and calling them “donkeys” for staying. The videos have sparked an online spat with France and raise concerns about AI‑driven disinformation in the election campaign.

title: Paris Imposes Nightly Curfew in Select Areas Until Monday
content:
A curfew has been extended in selected areas of Paris, effective every night from 11:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. The restriction remains in place until Monday morning. The measure, issued by the Paris police prefecture and published on Thursday, was put in force following the violence and looting that occurred over the weekend.

The same day, a student‑organized protest in Paris proceeded with hundreds in attendance. The demonstration had followed four weeks of earlier protests before the October 17 rallies. A police ban on the event was lifted after an emergency court injunction, allowing the protest to take place. FRANCE 24’s Mark Owen spoke with Alice Cohen‑Morzadec, International Spokesperson of “L’Union étudiante.”
summary: The curfew has been extended in certain areas of Paris, every night from 11:00 p. M.

title: Can weak economic growth threaten Europe's sophisticated social system?
content:
Europe faces the challenge of maintaining one of the world’s most ambitious social systems while its economic growth lags behind major competitors.  

The issue, according to former European Commissioner for Trade and former World Trade Organization Director‑General Pascal Lamy, lies at the core of the continent’s rising economic and political tensions.  

Lamy argues that the problem extends beyond France’s current turmoil, pointing to a widening gap between Europe’s social commitments and its ability to generate the economic growth required to sustain them.
summary: Pascal Lamy, former European Commissioner for Trade and former WTO Director-General, says Europe faces a widening disconnect between its social commitments and its ability to generate the economic growth needed to sustain them. He argues that this gap threatens the continent's ability to maintain its ambitious social model amid mounting economic and political tensions.

content:
A 7.0‑magnitude earthquake struck China’s remote Tibet region on Thursday, according to state media. The tremor was strong enough to trigger widespread damage across the area.

At least 16 people have died and dozens more were injured, with hundreds of houses collapsing in the quake’s aftermath.
summary: At least 16 people died and dozens more were injured after a 7.0 earthquake struck China’s remote Tibet region on Thursday, according to state media. Hundreds of houses collapsed during the tremor.

title: Oil prices hit five-month high as Gulf attacks threaten supply
content:
Oil prices rose to a five‑month high on Thursday after attacks in Saudi Arabia and incidents involving tankers in the Strait of Hormuz raised concerns about further disruptions to global crude supplies. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it struck four vessels in the northern Gulf and that three additional vessels hit mines near the strait.

The benchmark Brent crude increased 3%, reaching $112 a barrel, the first time it had traded at that level since 18 May. The price jump reflects market reactions to the reported maritime attacks and the perceived threat to oil flow from the region.

title: First human case of Shamonda virus identified in France
content:
A man in France has become the first known human case of Shamonda virus, a bunyavirus transmitted by bites from infected midges. Authorities are investigating whether the virus, which is typically found in livestock, contributed to the man’s death.

The Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety notes that in cattle, sheep and goats the virus can cause diarrhoea, loss of appetite, reduced milk production, abortions and congenital abnormalities in newborn animals. Investigations continue to determine the role of the virus in the fatal human infection.
summary: A man in France has become the first known human to contract Shamonda virus, a bunyavirus spread by bites from infected midges. Investigations are under way to determine whether the virus, which can cause diarrhoea, loss of appetite, reduced milk yield, abortions and congenital abnormalities in cattle, sheep and goats, contributed to his death.

title: Lewis Hamilton wants to race until early 2030s to compete in Rwanda's African Grand Prix
content:
Lewis Hamilton, the 41‑year‑old seven‑time Formula One world champion, has said he hopes to keep racing until the early 2030s so he can compete in the African Grand Prix. Hamilton described the event as a “dream” and said he believes it is right for F1 to hold a race in Rwanda despite criticism of the country’s human‑rights record.

Formula One confirmed that Rwanda will host the African Grand Prix after a ten‑year agreement was reached for a purpose‑built circuit. The venue will be in Bugesera, about 25 miles south of Kigali, and the first race is scheduled for the early 2030s. The event will mark the sport’s return to Africa for the first time since the 1993 Grand Prix at Kyalami in South Africa.
summary: Lewis Hamilton wants to race until early 2030s to compete in Rwanda's African Grand Prix.

title: Glee’s pro-LGBTQ+ vision captured 2010s hope. Can a reboot handle Trump’s America? | Alim Kheraj
content: The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needs For months, Ryan Murphy has been discussing Glee. In July, he expressed his love for the musical comedy drama he created. In September, he said that he had finished writing a pilot for a potential reboot, adding that he had reached out to some of the cast about a reunion. And now it is official : Disney+ and Hulu have commissioned a Glee revival. Glee, which ran for six seasons between 2009 and 2015, was a cultural juggernaut during its initial tenure. The show won six Emmys, four Golden Globes and made stars of actors including Lea Michele, Jonathan Groff, Chris Colfer, Darren Criss and the late Cory Monteith and Naya Rivera. Centred on the trials of New Directions, a scrappy show choir at the fictional McKinley high school in Ohio, the show became known for its peppy covers of show tunes, 80s power pop hits such as Journey’s Don’t Stop Believin’ (a Glee signature), 2010s chart-toppers and some truly baffling mashups (the amalgamation of Scissor Sisters’ Let’s Have a Kiki and Turkey Lurkey Time from Promises, Promises remains … a choice).
summary: The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needs For months, Ryan Murphy has been discussing Glee.

title: Bruno Guimarães says sleepless nights leaving Newcastle, looks forward to Arsenal
content:
Bruno Guimarães said goodbye at St James’ Park with tears, admitting he lay awake at night as the emotions swirled. The Brazil midfielder described the move as a test of steeliness, fixing his eyes on a new prize even though he knew his feelings would well up.

The summer had been tumultuous for Guimarães. After a personal World Cup highlight, he missed a crucial penalty in the last‑16 loss to Norway. The decision to leave Newcastle meant breaking hearts at the club where he had joined from Lyon in January 2022.

Newcastle had delivered memorable moments for him, including Champions League qualifications and a Carabao Cup triumph in 2025 that ended a 70‑year wait for a domestic trophy. Yet the prospect of competing regularly for the game’s top honours drew him to Arsenal, where he hopes to find the same love he left behind.
summary: Bruno Guimarães said he lay awake at night as he said goodbye to Newcastle, the club he joined from Lyon in January 2022 and with which he won the 2025 Carabao Cup. After a World Cup that included a penalty miss in the last‑16 loss to Norway, he is set to join Arsenal.

title: McDermott blames World Cup format after England face exit
content:
Brian McDermott has suggested England’s chances of advancing to the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals may be over, citing the tournament’s format and an initial defeat to Tonga. The head coach remarked that the team needed to “hit the ground running,” a standard they did not meet. Reaching the semi-finals now requires significant victories and assistance from Tonga.

The World Cup has shrunk to ten teams, down from sixteen four years prior. This reduction occurred largely for financial reasons after hosts Australia stepped in following France’s withdrawal. The change resulted in a unique format that creates varying levels of jeopardy for different nations depending on their group placement.
summary: Head coach Brian McDermott admitted England's hopes of reaching the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals may be over, citing the tournament's format and their opening loss to Tonga. title: Ruti Aga banned for six years over fake prescription
content:
Ethiopian marathon runner Ruti Aga has received a six-year ban after anti-doping investigators determined she submitted a fake prescription to explain a failed drug test. The Athletics Integrity Unit announced the sanction on Thursday, noting that Aga tested positive for the banned substance methylprednisolone following her victory in a half-marathon in China in March.

Investigators found that the prescription was signed by a family member rather than a doctor and referenced a clinic that did not exist. Aga, who won the Tokyo marathon in 2019 and has finished on the podium at the Berlin and New York marathons, is now suspended from competition for the next six years.
summary: Marathon runner Ruti Aga received a six-year ban after submitting a fake prescription to explain a failed drug test. The prescription was signed by a family member and named a clinic that did not exist.

Organisers described this as the most ambitious start in the race’s history, with six days of competition spanning Scotland, England’s Lake District, Peak District, Lancashire, and Yorkshire, as well as Wales and central London. The route is expected to attract millions of spectators.

The men’s race will include stages in Britain, time trials, and a volcano. Meanwhile, the Tour de France Femmes will conclude on Puy de Dôme. Organisers stated that Britain offers a symbol that ties the races together.
summary: Race organizers unveiled the 2027 Tour de France routes in Paris, featuring a Grand Départ across Scotland, England, and Wales. The women's race will conclude on Puy de Dôme, while the six-day British start is expected to attract millions of spectators.

title: Sri Lanka chase 430 to beat England despite Brook's record ODI 202
content:
Sri Lanka defeated England in a historic One Day International at Rawalpindi, successfully chasing a target of 430. This victory marked the second-highest successful chase in ODI history, trailing only the 438-run chase from twenty years ago. The result came despite England captain Harry Brook scoring the fastest double century in ODI history, as his record innings proved insufficient to secure a win for his team.

The match featured a dramatic turnaround for Sri Lanka, who recovered from an early collapse of 24 for two. Pavan Rathnayake top-scored with 130 runs, while Dasun Shanaka and Avishka Fernando both contributed 97. Shanaka’s aggressive performance included eight sixes, helping the team overcome its initial struggles. Although England briefly regained momentum late in the innings, Sri Lanka secured the victory with one ball to spare. The final over saw Liyanage hit a six to complete the chase, cementing the historic nature of the contest.
summary: Sri Lanka successfully chased a target of 430 in Rawalpindi, achieving the second-highest chase in ODI history to defeat England. England captain Harry Brook scored the fastest double century in ODI history, but Sri Lanka's innings, led by Pavan Rathnayake's 130, secured the win.

title: Jackdaw gasfield approval part of UK's net‑zero plan, says PM Andy Burnham
content:
On Wednesday, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved the start of gas production at the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. The decision follows years of intense debate, with strong positions on both sides of the issue.

The new field will supply gas that will begin heating homes and powering businesses this winter. In the longer term, it is expected to raise domestic gas production by about 6 %, strengthening the UK’s energy security for more than a decade. The project is projected to protect hundreds of jobs in Scotland and add almost £3 billion to the UK economy over its lifetime.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated that the approval does not compromise Labour’s commitment to a cleaner, greener future and that the United Kingdom will still meet its net‑zero target. He invites readers to submit up to 300‑word responses to be considered for publication in the letters section.
summary: Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved gas production at the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. The approval will boost domestic gas production by about 6%, support energy supply for more than a decade, protect hundreds of jobs in Scotland and add almost £3bn to the UK economy.

He specifically committed to blocking new North Sea licences to keep Britain on track for its environmental goals.

title: UK Government Urges Citizens to Stockpile Nine Litres of Water and Three Days of Food
content:
The UK government has launched the Be Ready campaign to help households prepare for emergencies linked to the climate crisis, technological dependence, and hostile‑state threats. The campaign urges every Briton to stockpile supplies that can sustain a household for 72 hours.

Under the new guidance, residents are advised to keep at least nine litres of bottled water and a three‑day supply of food in their homes. The supplies are intended to support families during weather events, cyber incidents, or other serious emergencies.

The campaign reflects growing official concern about the increasing frequency of extreme weather, the vulnerability of digital infrastructure, and the potential for state‑sponsored threats to disrupt normal life.
summary: The UK government has issued new guidance urging every Briton to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days' worth of food.
