Legislation creating Chiricahua National Park was sent to the White House and signed by President Donald Trump on Tuesday. The bill passed Congress with bipartisan support and is now the 64th national park in the United States.

title: Arizona storms topple trees, knock down poles and produce golf‑ball sized hail
content:
Violent storms that moved through central Arizona overnight knocked over utility poles and carried thunder and heavy winds. In one central Arizona community, trees fell onto homes and utility poles were knocked down by a possible tornado during the series of storms that continued into Thursday.

The National Weather Service said the storms were capable of causing hail and wind damage and were traveling through central Arizona early on Thursday. It also issued some flood watches and noted the possibility of tornadoes.

title: Study Finds PICU Parent Support May Modestly Lower PTSD and Depression
content:
Researchers examined the impact of psychosocial support on parents after their child’s stay in a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU). A systematic search of five major academic databases identified eight randomized controlled trials that evaluated various interventions for parents of PICU patients. The interventions studied included visits to follow‑up clinics, psychological screening with referral, telephone‑based psychoeducation, palliative care consultations, and acceptance and commitment therapy delivered via videoconference.

The analysis, published in Intensive and Critical Care Nursing, found that these mental‑health supports may modestly reduce post‑traumatic stress disorder and depressive symptoms in parents. The study highlights the potential benefits of structured psychosocial care for families coping with the lasting psychological effects of a child’s PICU admission.

Researchers identified the YAP1–TEAD–TET1 axis, which promotes DNA demethylation and activates multiple oncogenes in hepatocellular carcinoma.

title: Marine life in Gulf of Mexico still not fully recovered from 2010 BP oil spill
content:

The April 2010 explosion of an offshore drilling unit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast released 134 million gallons of oil, triggering the largest marine oil spill in history.

The study describes the disaster as causing “sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance” of marine life that have persisted for more than a decade. It also notes that the spill killed 11 people and injured 17 others.

title: Three things you should know about permafrost
content:
Three things you should know about permafrost

Permafrost, the permanently frozen layer of soil that lies beneath roughly 15 % of land in the Northern Hemisphere, has been largely overlooked in climate discussions. It was formed mainly during the last ice age, trapping organic material that has remained locked away for thousands of years. As global temperatures rise, this material is thawing, allowing microbes to break down the organic matter and release carbon dioxide and methane—both powerful greenhouse gases that accelerate warming. The Arctic permafrost area has already shrunk by about 12 % since 1850, and the rate of loss has accelerated over the past 50 years. Yet most models used in United Nations climate reports include only the gradual loss of permafrost, omitting the abrupt thaw and collapse that can follow heat waves and fires. Because of this omission, scientists warn that current projections may underestimate how quickly the planet could warm.

Wildfires, a natural component of boreal forest ecosystems, are becoming more intense due to climate change. These fires can speed up permafrost thaw, potentially releasing the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by the end of the century. In remote parts of Canada and Alaska, the prevailing policy is to allow fires to burn unless they threaten human habitats. Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are mapping burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska, identifying areas where fires are likely to spread and where specific permafrost types—such as the deep, carbon‑dense Yedoma from the late Pleistocene—could release the most emissions. Proposed responses include prescribed fires, a practice used by Indigenous groups for millennia to reduce the risk of large blazes, as well as early detection and suppression efforts.

The carbon cycle of permafrost is highly complex. Approximately 1.5 trillion tons of carbon are stored in permafrost, roughly twice the amount in the atmosphere. While thawing releases greenhouse gases, other processes may offset some of that loss. For instance, as temperatures rise, plants can expand northward, sequestering atmospheric carbon as they grow. Researchers are still working to quantify how much carbon is lost from thaw and how much can be recovered, taking into account factors such as fire severity, local climate, and permafrost type. The more the planet warms, the more these intertwined natural phenomena will challenge our understanding. This article appears in The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter.
summary: How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.

title: Making the case for context-aware AI
content: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes. For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know. The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling. This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents. Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis. Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized. Two words for you: context matters. My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis. Welcome, Devavrat. Devavrat Shah: Hello, Megan. Thanks for having me here. Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today. Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale? Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question. And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned. As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises. The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization. We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes. There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency. In either of them, we have some processes in place. You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first. Many of us help coordinate those things. Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task. And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision. Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can’t just do that in a vacuum. And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come. Megan: Right. To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making. If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play? Devavrat: Fantastic. Let’s just take the setting I was describing. We are trying to automate a role or support a role or augment a role depending on the type of decision, depending upon type of task. And let’s for a second imagine that all these, as they’re called, frontier labs have built these amazing models and amazing AI infrastructure so that everything that’s happened in the universe and it’s likely to happen in the universe is all there. Now, we have a small decision that we want to make for that very specific context is there. And without having access to that, this massive system, this extremely bright person would figure that out eventually by asking lots of questions, the way we do it as humans, and then finally do the right thing. The problem is to get to that, it will do so much compute at some level that to get simple tasks done, we are spending massive amount of compute. So that’s scenario one. In reality, that’s not going to be the scenario, and we’ll miss some important context, important constraint, important guardrail, and then we’ll make a mistake. And sometimes that mistake can be okay. It’s like me giving you a recommendation saying, go restaurant A, and maybe you may not enjoy the dinner, versus sometimes mistakes will be very, very expensive. That is me telling you what the financial forecast is and somehow that leads to the company’s doom. Megan: Right. So in an enterprise setting, these are really business critical decisions that are being made. So the impact is that much more if we get this wrong, isn’t it? And on a practical level then, what are the different ways that organizations can add in this context layer we’re talking about? How does Celonis, for example, deliver that operational context via a real time digital twin of an organization? Devavrat: Absolutely. I think if it might be useful just to double click on the history of Celonis. As you know, Celonis, as an organization, came into existence with the mission, with the goal of helping organizations adhere to their ideal processes, build better processes, enable people to work with multiple processes in an intertwined manner. And that’s where their primary, let’s call it a DNA, has been about what I would call process intelligence. Take how enterprises help put multiple things together, digitize them, enable people to get their processes better, understand where the issues are, and then how do you re-engineer the process within organizations so that things can happen better. Now, if you want to bring decision intelligence into this, each atomic step of this process that was potentially was done before by experts, people, now we want agents to help us enable that. And that’s where knowing this context of a process within enterprise and then bringing AI agents along with that, what I would like to call it as a roled agents, exactly provide the right way to bring decision intelligence to enterprises. And this is how Celonis brings context to help enterprise make better decision. Megan: Right. And then in terms of how this works as well, how does the context layer relate to both the layer below, that’s the systems of record layer, and also the layer above, that identic layer? Devavrat: That’s a fantastic question, Megan. The layer below primarily is, if we call it system of record, primarily it’s the workflow tools that are there and then the event logs that they generate around it. The layer above is either business user experts consuming information, or they’re consuming that information maybe through agents working on top of that context layer. And this is where the way context model, as Celonis calls it, is designed is to do three things simultaneously. One is to get the right abstraction of the layer below, so that the right pieces of the process can be agentified. Two is to bring the rolled agents for each of these pieces in a structured guardrailed manner. And then the three is to be agent first so that if there are other agentic infrastructure that are already talking to it, they can naturally talk to it so that then they can bring the right output for humans or experts to review, look at it, approve, and maybe then at times automate. Megan: Fantastic. And for all the benefits that we’re talking about with this, are there also challenges when it comes to implementing a context layer? For example, do most organizations have the right data in place to provide AI with the context it needs? And if not, I wonder what some of the practical steps are that they might need to take to address that. Devavrat: It’s again, a crucial question to make this real. We can imagine an ideal world, but if we cannot reach the ideal world, then it’s just ideal. So now in this setting, as we discussed the three layers, one being the layer which is the layer below system of record and workflow tools. In some sense, those things already exist. They don’t need to be complete. They don’t need to be in the cleanest possible manner. The way context model is designed with agentic’s architecture, it manages to connect to those things and make sense of it. And then things on top is very much in control of Celonis’s infrastructure, so it’s not that complicated. The crucial thing here though is when one goes to enterprise, when one opens up, let’s say a system of record or workflow tool, event logs or things like that, one has to go through, what I would call, classical InfoSec to make sure that you can trust a vendor’s software that’s coming into your organization. And I think that is the primary process that is a step between, before and after, if I may call it. Megan: Right. So that’s the real crucial step for people to be taking here. And as AI agents with context are able to make more complex, more accurate hopefully decisions, I wonder what you think the role of human intelligence and input will be moving forward, and how can organizations perhaps strike the balance between the two? Devavrat: There are the benefits and then there are the challenges. Benefits are clear. If you have right AI agents in a right role manner going through your decision processes, hopefully they’re doing it quicker and hence your decisions are taken earlier so that your opportunity cost is not lost. You are taking decisions in time, you can plan much better, et cetera, et cetera. This is especially useful when you have to take very manual, repetitive, grungy tasks where access to workforce, coordination between people become crucial parts of the decision process. In a sense, that’s where the huge value can come in. The flip side of that is that means that people won’t be doing that. On the other hand, the other type of decision that we always make, which are strategic decisions. It could be a small strategic decision, it could be large strategic decision, but the strategic decisions that typically most organizations don’t have bandwidth to take to think, that opportunity would open up and that’s where likely lots of humans and experts would engage more. In a sense, now they would have better support helping them rationally think through what are the choices that they have, how do different choices compare? And then at the end of the day, it’s organization’s role to decide which of the option to take because it belongs to their interest in mind where they want to go. And so in a sense, there will be what I would call shift of workforce in terms of instead of doing a lot more repetitive, a lot less repetitive, but a lot more strategic work and that’s where people will have to spend time. The other place where I am personally very optimistic is like every technology change creates new work that it’s difficult to predict at the time of change. My hope is that there will be another type of opportunity and work that will be created where we’ll be engaging our workforce. Goes without saying, this would mean that we will have to carefully think through reeducating or educating some of our workforce thoughtfully. And I think as an academic in me, as an educator in me, I really feel that the timescale at which these changes are happening are so fast. So we need to also act in a similar manner. Megan: For any decision maker listening to this, how should they start implementing these changes? For example, how can they prepare their workforce? What role should governance play as well? Devavrat: Okay, that’s a great question. If you want to start, the first thing you need to do is identify a decision where you want to bring intelligence. Let’s identify the process around it. Let’s identify each step of the process. Let’s take the most crucial, difficult step in that. Let’s try to bring AI agents to help you to do that. And then from there you go and then let’s measure how much speed are we getting, how much value are we getting? And that’ll help us understand whether this was worth it. So that’s one. Second is governance. Well, we’re going to bring AI in this prescriptive manner for each task in a role. That means that for that role, we can tell what it can or cannot do very clearly. And Celonis prescribes certified role agents for these things. This helps you clearly have an understanding of what sort of contract would be for this. And the third thing, which is people, and now this is where it’s really important, is a part which gets automated, but then there’s a part where experts will be in the loop and this is where they need to understand the outputs of AI, how do you work with that and what its implication would be? And this is where some AI education is needed and then some tool education is needed. Megan: Yes, absolutely. The pace is incredible, isn’t it, in this space? And speaking of, I suppose if we could close with a look ahead, given the right context, of course, what are the use cases perhaps for enterprise AI that are on the horizon that you think could be most impactful or perhaps what you’re simply most excited about? Devavrat: I think I would categorize them into three types. They’re all decision intelligence, decision-making, but there are three types. One, what I would call many repetitive manual labor-intensive, so that’s one. Two, what I would call coordination style tasks. A lot of work that we do right now as an information workforce that’s spent in coordination, that’s why email spreadsheets, et cetera. A lot of that would be done much better, much quicker and less boring, so to speak. And then the third is where, especially as a support to human decision-makers to provide strategic support augmentation, and that’s a third type of decisions that would be done. If I think of any planning process in enterprises, so financial planning, workforce planning, marketing, sales, product, anything, all of those are business critical decisions that we make that take annual planning process, take annual time. Now maybe it should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly. Megan: That’d be fantastic, wouldn’t it? Fantastic. Thank you so much for that brilliant conversation, Devavrat. That was Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England. title: Microsoft says its AI tool diagnoses conditions up to four times more accurately than doctors
content:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman announced that the company has developed an AI-powered tool capable of diagnosing medical conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors. Suleyman described this development as the realization of a long-held promise by AI leaders to improve lives through healthcare applications. The company’s findings were published in the journal Science on Thursday.

The study’s results are based on tests comparing Microsoft’s AI system against human physicians using scenarios drawn from medical case reports and emergency department data. To conduct these comparisons, Microsoft compiled the cases into its own benchmark.
summary: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman said the company has created an AI-powered diagnostic tool that can diagnose conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors. The findings were published Thursday in the journal Science based on tests comparing the AI system with physicians using medical case reports and emergency department data.

title: Tesla in Full Self-Driving mode kills 71-year-old crossing I-80 in Vallejo
content:
A 71‑year‑old man was killed after being hit by a Tesla operating in Full Self‑Driving (FSD) mode while crossing Interstate 80 in Vallejo, California, at approximately 2:30 a.m. on Thursday, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. The California Highway Patrol said a dash‑cam video showed the Tesla applying its brakes and steering left in an attempt to avoid the pedestrian, yet the vehicle’s right‑front portion struck the man.

The CHP added that authorities believe at least one additional vehicle may have struck the pedestrian after the Tesla, though further details were not provided.
summary: A 71-year-old man was fatally struck by a Tesla operating in Full Self-Driving mode while crossing I-80 in Vallejo, California at about 2:30 AM on Thursday. Dash‑cam video showed the vehicle braking and steering left before its right front portion hit the pedestrian, and authorities believe another vehicle also struck the man after the Tesla.

title: EA shuts down BioWare, cancels Mass Effect game; leaked trailer appears on Reddit
content:
EA announced yesterday that it had shut down BioWare and canceled the studio’s new Mass Effect game that was in development. The decision came after the company’s broader restructuring of its game‑development portfolio.

A trailer that appears to represent the cancelled title was posted on Reddit today. The video is labeled “in‑engine footage” and uses “pre‑production assets,” according to a message at its start. It centers on an ex‑soldier speaking with a mysterious Asari character who approaches him at a bar, and it includes a flashback to a fight that echoes the gameplay of the original Mass Effect trilogy. The clip features humans and alien species mingling and brief action sequences, all of which feel distinctly Mass Effect.
summary: EA shut down BioWare and canceled the studio's new Mass Effect game in development, and a trailer representing the game was posted on Reddit. The trailer uses in‑engine footage and pre‑production assets, showing an ex‑soldier speaking with a mysterious Asari in a bar and a flashback to a fight reminiscent of the original trilogy.

title: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg bets future on Muse AI agent after earnings call
content:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg outlined a vision of an autonomous network of AI agents that would handle tasks such as shopping, work, and communication on users’ behalf. During the company’s quarterly earnings call on Wednesday night, he emphasized that the firm’s future is being built around Muse, the personal AI agent that Meta made available to the general public last month.

Zuckerberg indicated that investors would likely focus on whether he himself is prepared for the scenario in which people primarily interact through AI‑mediated proxies. The discussion highlighted the early stage of Muse’s deployment and its central role in Meta’s strategic plans.
summary: Mark Zuckerberg said on Meta's quarterly earnings call that the company is staking its future on Muse, the personal AI agent released to the public last month. He outlined a vision where autonomous AI agents handle shopping, work and communication for users.

title: Delta 2.0 emulator update adds iPhone Duo optimization and new features
content:
The Delta gaming emulator has been updated to version 2.0, bringing a range of new features and support enhancements. Among the additions are Sega Genesis game compatibility, animated controller skins, custom Pokémon DLC experiences, and a redesigned user interface built around “Liquid Glass.”  

A key focus of the update is optimization for Apple’s iPhone Duo, a foldable device with a shape reminiscent of a Nintendo DS. The upgrade tailors controller skins for every orientation in both portrait and landscape modes, according to Delta creator Riley Testut, who discussed the changes with The Verge.  

Delta 2.0’s support for the iPhone Duo is highlighted as a standout improvement for users interested in emulating Nintendo DS titles on the foldable handset. The update also includes broader performance and compatibility refinements across the emulator’s existing features.
summary: Delta 2.0 adds support for Apple’s iPhone Duo and includes Sega Genesis games, animated controller skins, custom Pokémon DLC experiences, and a UI built for Liquid Glass. Delta creator Riley Testut said the update optimizes controller skins for every pose in both portrait and landscape orientations.

title: UNEP says 1.5°C limit already exceeded, shifts focus to limiting overshoot
content:
In 2015, all but two countries agreed to try to keep global temperatures from rising more than 1.5 °C above pre‑industrial levels. Since that agreement, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) says most nations have treated the target as aspirational, and the United States has alternately withdrawn from and recommitted to the pact.  

On Wednesday, UNEP announced that it no longer considers keeping warming below 1.5 °C a viable goal. The agency now proposes to focus on limiting both the duration and magnitude of any overshoot of the 1.5 °C threshold. Achieving that, UNEP says, will require dramatic emissions cuts immediately and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the end of the century.  

The organization notes that, depending on the baseline and temperature reconstruction used, the world is either very close to or has already exceeded the 1.5 °C milestone, and that the exceptionally strong current El Niño event is likely to push temperatures over the limit regardless of the record chosen.
summary: UNEP acknowledged that keeping global warming below 1.5°C is no longer viable. It said future action must limit the duration and magnitude of any overshoot, requiring dramatic emissions cuts and removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of CO₂ before the end of the century.

title: 300+ Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH and capture plaintext email
content:
A researcher reported on Tuesday that unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and altered them to favor unencrypted email traffic while redirecting SSH connections through servers under the attackers’ control. The intrusion began in late August, according to Tor volunteers, when the perpetrators used a reused valid password to gain access to a Tor management server.

After breaching the management server, the attackers installed Ebury, a Linux backdoor first identified 12 years ago. They then connected from that server to a second Tor server named Switzerland2 via SSH, employing an RSA key that investigators could not locate among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative access to Switzerland2, the attackers also deployed Ebury on that system.

Finally, the intruders reconfigured the settings of two exit nodes hosted on Switzerland2, completing the manipulation of the compromised Tor infrastructure.
summary: 300+ Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH and capture plaintext email.

title: GM says it remains all‑in on EVs and autonomy as Super Cruise expands to most models
content:
General Motors used its recent GM Forward event to reaffirm its commitment to electrification, autonomous driving and vehicle quality. Executives said the company’s “hands‑off, eyes‑off” Super Cruise system will be broadened to almost the entire model range, extending beyond the Escalade IQ announced last year to include pickup trucks and crossovers.

Sterling Anderson, GM’s head of product, noted that Super Cruise is being tested at a rate of one million miles (approximately 1.6 million km) each month in both virtual simulations and real‑world driving. The company framed this effort as part of a broader goal for vehicles to not only transport occupants but also perform additional tasks for them.

Ars Technica disclosed that GM covered its travel from Detroit to New York and lodging to attend the event, and clarified that the outlet does not accept paid editorial content. The announcement underscores GM’s intention to stay “all‑in” on electric vehicles and autonomous technology despite external criticism.
summary: At the GM Forward event, executives announced that the hands‑off Super Cruise system will be rolled out to nearly every vehicle, including trucks and crossovers, with testing at about 1 million miles per month. The company also reaffirmed its focus on electrification, autonomy and improving vehicle quality.

title: Rings of Power S3 trailer shows Sauron recruiting future Ringwraiths
content:
Amazon Prime Video’s “Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” will return next month with its third season. Earlier this year the series was previewed with a teaser at San Diego Comic‑Con, and the network has now released the full trailer for the upcoming season.

The trailer depicts a rising Sauron leading an army of Orcs and pursuing conquest of Middle‑Earth, while elves, dwarves and men struggle to oppose him. It also introduces a group of human men who will become the Ringwraiths; the showrunners refer to these characters as the Nazgnagol (“Rings‑servant”).

Prime Video previously secured the rights to the Tolkien material from the Tolkien estate and committed to multiple seasons. Season three is set seven years after the events of season two and opens amid an intensified war between the elves and Sauron.
summary: The official full trailer for the third season of “The Rings of Power” reveals a rising Sauron leading an Orc army and the human men who will become Ringwraiths, called Nazgnagol by the showrunners. The season, set seven years after season two, returns next month with the war between elves and Sauron at its height.

content: Amazon warned that vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language, discovered with AI tools, are “broadly exploited” as governments and companies scramble to secure their systems. title: VBoy Color emulator adds full-color palette to Nintendo Virtual Boy games
content:
A new emulator called VBoy Color expands on the earlier Red Viper Virtual Boy emulator by introducing a tile‑based palette system that supports many more colors in each frame. According to the emulator’s readme files, game‑specific “Color Packs” can assign a distinct four‑color palette to each 8×8 tile, rather than merely swapping the original four shades of red for four different hues.

The approach lets the emulator differentiate objects that shared the same red tones in the original hardware. For example, in Mario Clash the emulator can render green pipes, grey platforms and red brick walls with separate palettes, and in titles such as Jack Bros. or Vertical Force it improves contrast between the player character and busy red backgrounds. The resulting visuals are described as reminiscent of a Game Boy Color‑style display, as if Nintendo had originally equipped the Virtual Boy with a full‑color screen.
summary: VBoy Color is an emulator that uses a tile‑based palette system to assign a distinct four‑color palette to each 8×8 tile in Virtual Boy games. This lets titles such as Mario Clash, Jack Bros. and Vertical Force display many more colors and improve contrast compared with the original red‑on‑red display.

title: Guinea-Bissau rejects US‑funded hepatitis B newborn vaccine trial
content:
Government officials in Guinea‑Bissau have formally rejected a clinical trial that would be conducted by Danish researchers and financed by the United States. The study was intended to investigate alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn dose of the hepatitis B vaccine, a dose that is currently recommended worldwide and has been used safely for decades.

In an email to Ars Technica, lead researcher Christine Stabell Benn of the Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark said that Guinea‑Bissau’s Council of Ministers “formally reaffirmed its non‑acceptance of the study on 16 October.” The rejection was reported after judicial police in the country raided the Bandim Health offices and seized vaccines; the police action followed the council’s decision.
summary: Government officials in Guinea‑Bissau formally rejected a US‑funded clinical trial by Danish researchers that aimed to investigate alleged nonspecific harms of the newborn hepatitis B vaccine. The Council of Ministers reaffirmed its non‑acceptance on 16 October, and judicial police subsequently raided the Bandim Health Project offices and seized vaccines.

title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion fine after New Mexico rejects settlement
content:
A jury in New Mexico found Meta guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer‑protection laws, ordering the company to pay a $25 billion fine. The penalty is the largest ever imposed on Meta, according to the court’s ruling.

The fine followed New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez’s decision not to join an $18 billion settlement that Meta had reached earlier this year with attorneys general in almost every other state. Torrez’s refusal left New Mexico to pursue its own case against the tech giant.

In his opinion issued Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew noted that there is no “bright line rule” for setting a penalty for Meta’s repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 over issues such as data control, third‑party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.
summary: Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found it guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws. The penalty follows New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez’s decision not to join an $18 billion multistate settlement Meta reached earlier this year.

title: Finland orders Google to halt work after illegal felling of 250,000 trees
content: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland. Now they are all gone. After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.
summary: Google was ordered to stop work at two sites in Finland after it illegally cleared about 250,000 trees from a 330‑hectare forest near Muhos to build a datacentre. Residents say brown water from the cleared site is flowing into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.

title: The Audacity TV series satirizes AI tech titans with Succession‑style drama
content: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat. This acerbic and all-too-timely Silicon Valley satire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. He’s a self-proclaimed “inventor of the future” who also happens to be a morally bankrupt man-baby. “Duncan is worth about half a billion,” says Glatzer. “Naturally, that’s not enough. He desperately wants to be a billionaire and ascend to what we call ‘God Mountain’. But he’s no God.”
summary: The Audacity TV series satirizes AI tech titans with Succession‑style drama.

title: Websites worldwide face millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
content:
Websites around the globe have experienced millions of attempts to exploit a newly disclosed vulnerability in the PHP programming language, according to cybersecurity firms. The flaw, which affects the language that underpins roughly 70 % of all websites, was first reported on Wednesday.

In response, several governments and private companies have taken their sites offline to apply patches before any successful attacks could occur. U.S. officials have warned that the vulnerability could enable attackers to seize control of web servers, exfiltrate data and disrupt services. The coordinated pull‑offline actions aim to mitigate those risks while the PHP code is being corrected.

title: Three‑day US‑Israeli attack on Iran unlikely to radically change conflict
content:
Ahead of upcoming U.S. and Israeli elections, a 3‑day joint attack on Iran has been argued would not radically change the conflict. In a recent discussion, Jean‑Emile Jammine welcomed Federico Donelli, an associate professor of International Relations at the University of Trieste, to speak on the issue.

Donelli challenged the assumption that a short, intensive offensive would produce a decisive political outcome. He said the real question is whether military pressure is intended to constrain Iran’s capacity or to push Iran to the negotiating table, and whether such pressure can be translated into a sustainable political outcome without provoking a wider regional crisis. He also reminded that Iran still retains leverage over the United States.
summary: Ahead of US and Israeli elections, a three‑day joint attack on Iran is said to be unlikely to radically change the conflict. Associate Professor Federico Donelli of the University of Trieste said short intensive strikes may not produce a decisive political outcome and noted that Iran still has leverage over the United States.

title: Russia bombards Kyiv with missiles hours after agreeing to resume talks with Ukraine
content:
Russia launched a massive “demonstrative” attack on Kyiv, firing ballistic missiles overnight just hours after President Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations following talks with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff.  

The strike killed at least two people and wounded 22, including four children. Targets hit in the Ukrainian capital included the southern bridge over the Dnipro River, civilian houses, energy infrastructure, an ambulance station, office buildings and a clinic. Experts said the assault appears aimed at destroying energy infrastructure before winter and that U.S. “appeasement and flattery” will not achieve peace.

title: Macron bans “illegitimate” protests, permits recognized group demos with route changes
content:
French President Emmanuel Macron announced that “illegitimate” demonstrations would be banned over the coming days as France attempts to curb civil unrest. The decision follows a surge of street violence on the fringes of cost‑of‑living protests that some of the country’s worst in years. Macron made the statement after a meeting with intelligence officials and senior ministers.

The report highlights that approximately 24% of the planet’s reefs across more than 80 countries are already critically endangered. However, when the projected impacts of global heating are factored in, the percentage of reefs at risk rises to 96%.

The data underscores the severe vulnerability of coral reefs worldwide, with the vast majority expected to suffer significant degradation within the coming decades if current heating trends continue.

title: WD report warns AI inference generates hidden storage costs up to 130x output size
content:
Executives often picture AI costs in terms of GPUs, power consumption and silicon shortages, but a recent WD analysis highlights that data‑storage expenses are a substantial, and frequently overlooked, component of AI infrastructure. The analysis notes that every inference request leaves behind data that must be retained, creating a continuous storage burden that grows as AI usage expands.

A concrete example comes from internal measurements of AI‑generated video. An 8‑second clip delivered to a user as a 3.97 MB 720p file generated more than 500 MB of backend data—including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups and safety records—representing a 130‑fold increase over the user‑visible file size. When enterprises produce longer, higher‑resolution video, the backend footprint can reach hundreds of gigabytes per clip, and the overall storage demand is accelerating. McKinsey projects AI inference demand to grow at a 35 % compound annual growth rate through 2030, outpacing the 22 % growth projected for training and eventually accounting for over 40 % of total data‑center demand.

A WD‑sponsored IDC white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision‑makers found that nearly 95 % of respondents observed an increase in data volume due to generative AI in the past year, with roughly 61 % reporting growth of 25 % or more. The same survey indicated that 96 % anticipate a need for faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG). A senior product manager at a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in the report said that additional storage serves as an optimization to keep GPUs busy, noting that “hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.”

The analysis warns that storage spending can outpace compute budgets. While compute budgets tend to follow predictable cycles, storage costs may rise 25 % year over year, eventually eclipsing the line items that receive the most attention. Because data generated during inference—model logs, synthetic outputs and results—remains retained, it can become an input for future AI workloads, turning archives that were once rarely accessed into active assets.

To address these challenges, organizations are urged to adopt an architecture that balances performance with capacity across warm, cool and cold storage tiers. The report recommends treating archives as reusable resources for RAG and inference, establishing clear data‑retention policies, and aligning storage procurement with the full AI data lifecycle rather than solely with training‑time performance needs. It also proposes three questions for budgeting teams: what is the data‑retention policy for AI‑generated content; is storage procurement tied to training performance or data lifecycle; and would storage costs double if AI usage doubled. According to the analysis, many organizations cannot answer these questions confidently, indicating a gap that should be closed before the next budgeting cycle.
summary: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs.

I did not expect this game to become a family fixture for the next several years as my kids got older and climbed up the online ranks in all six of its sports (plus the two that were added as free updates). Switch Sports is so beloved in my household that the release of Switch Sports Resort this week is the most anticipated gaming event of the year. To be fair, my children are a bit young for Grand Theft Auto. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings three of the six sports back – tennis, bowling, and volleyball – alongside golf and basketball. Then there are seven entirely new sports: boxing, table tennis, archery, thumb wrestling, skateboarding, jetski, and piloting a little prop plane. They are all intuitive, easy to get the hang of on the first or second attempt – some have more legs than others, in the long run – and all of them, crucially, are a little bit silly. Thumb wrestling in particular is cheerfully absurd, giving your characters gigantic thumbs on hands the size of their heads.
summary: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games.

content:

content:

Experiments using preclinical models and human pancreatic cells demonstrated that blocking specific proteins within this pathway helped protect beta cells from excessive cellular stress.

The findings, recently published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation, suggest a new strategy to preserve the cells responsible for regulating blood sugar. This approach may potentially offer a treatment option for type 2 diabetes.
summary: Researchers at Weill Cornell Medicine found that blocking proteins in a cellular stress pathway protects insulin‑producing beta cells from death. content:

Carr said that many journalists and broadcasters have been “amplifying or airing these polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis.” He urged stations to avoid “News Distortions” or “Broadcast Hoaxes” by refraining from airing polls that would violate regulatory obligations and to provide viewers with additional context and information about the polls they cover.

Carr cited recent examples, noting that a small polling outfit was exposed as a hoax this week and a similar incident occurred in August. He pointed out that news outlets have reported on these hoaxes, supplying the context he said is necessary.
